payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the image into pencil drawing
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the image show the original visual content rendered in a pencil-drawn style?
node.criteria: Pass if the image visibly represents its content as a pencil drawing; fail if there is sufficient evidence that no pencil-drawing transformation has occurred; unknown if the image or its style cannot be assessed reliably. Partial evidence of a pencil-drawn style is progress, not completion.
node.binding: Compare the supplied image with the requested transformation: assess whether its visual content is rendered in a pencil-drawn style. Do not require a particular pencil technique.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting while rendering them in a muted, grainy, pencil-like style with softened outlines and shading.
The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting but renders them with muted, desaturated tones and visible fine grain and sketch-like shading consistent with a pencil-drawn style.
The edited image preserves the original scene and visibly renders it with muted, sketch-like shading and pencil-textured outlines, consistent with a pencil-drawn style.
The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting while rendering them with muted, grainy, pencil-like shading and softened outlines, consistent with a pencil-drawing style.
The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting but renders them with muted, desaturated tones and visible fine grain and sketch-like shading consistent with a pencil-drawn style.

fulfillment: The node’s completion criterion is too permissive: it treats s1 passing as sufficient, and the repeated traces show that s1 is being passed for muted color, grain, and softened shading even when the image still retains photographic structure and shading. This collapses visible progress into full fulfillment and explains the repeated “yes” labels despite the partial reference. Refine the typed criterion so completion requires evidence that the scene is rendered as a drawing overall, not merely that it has pencil-like texture or desaturation; keep s2 as evidence of progress and preserve the existing partial/absent/unknown distinctions. Have the decision cite concrete visual evidence from the edited image and compare it with the source, rather than inheriting a support’s conclusion that a pencil-like treatment establishes completion. The traces are valid and queried with no transport or dependency failures, so this is a semantic threshold/binding issue, not missing evidence. Do not force “partial” from the reference label alone; use it only to flag that the current completion rule is over-crediting the observed treatment.
s2: The node is correctly scoped to detecting progress, but its pass result is being treated downstream as full fulfillment. Keep this support node’s criterion limited to whether a visible, relevant change moves the image toward pencil drawing; do not make it decide completion. In the supplied pair, the edited image has muted, near-monochrome colors and grainy, softened edges across the scene, while the original is vivid and photographic. Those are concrete signs of progress, but the edited image still retains photographic shading and structure, so they do not establish that the requested transformation is complete. Ensure the downstream decision distinguishes this partial progress from full fulfillment and cites the source comparison. The traces are valid and queried with no transport or dependency failures; this is a semantic threshold/routing issue, not missing evidence. Treat repeated high-confidence passes as a signal to inspect whether support evidence is being mistaken for completion, not as proof of completion or a reason to force the reference label.
